title: Revisiting Robustness in Graph Machine Learning

en.text: The standard story about graph neural networks (GNNs) is that they are dangerously easy to fool. Flip a handful of edges, and a model that looked accurate suddenly changes its mind. A decade of adversarial-robustness research has treated that fragility as the whole problem: the attacker makes a tiny, meaning-preserving change, and the model that keeps its prediction is the robust, trustworthy one. This ICLR 2023 paper from the Technical University of Munich points out that the story quietly assumes something we never actually check on graphs - that the small change really did preserve the node's meaning.

That assumption is doing a lot of work. An adversarial example is only adversarial if it leaves the input's true label untouched; otherwise a changed prediction is just a correct response to a genuinely different input. For images, a human can glance at the perturbed picture and confirm it still shows a cat. Graphs have no such visual check, so the community settled on a proxy: count how many edges were inserted or deleted, and call the perturbation "small" if that count stays under an l0 budget. The paper's central observation is that on real graphs, where most nodes have very few neighbors, even a tiny edge budget can rewire a node completely - and once you rewire a low-degree node, its true class may have already changed.

Read that way, a model that stubbornly keeps its old prediction is not being robust in any good sense. It is being wrong about an input whose ground truth has moved. The authors give this failure mode a name - over-robustness - and build the tools to measure it. Their headline finding is uncomfortable: every GNN they test is significantly over-robust, and a surprisingly large share of the robustness we routinely celebrate lies beyond the point where the node's semantics already flipped.

en.caption: Figure 1. On synthetic CSBM graphs, the dotted "semantic boundary" marks how many edge changes actually flip a node's true (most-likely) class, as a function of node degree. Every GNN (colored curves) only changes its own prediction far above that line - the entire shaded band between the two is robustness the model keeps after the semantics have already changed.

Project page: https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/daml/revisiting-robustness/
Why "count the edited edges" is not enough

The reason graphs are hard is that you cannot inspect a perturbed node the way you inspect a perturbed image. Prior work tried to make edge-counting more principled by adding proxies - keep the degree distribution roughly fixed, preserve homophily, and so on - so that a perturbation looks "unnoticeable." But none of those heuristics asks the one question that actually defines an adversarial example: did the node's ground-truth label survive the edit?

This gap matters because of a plain fact about real graphs: they are dominated by low-degree nodes. If a node has three neighbors and your budget lets you change three edges, you can detach it from its entire original neighborhood and wire it into a new one. Nothing about the degree distribution needs to look suspicious for the node's true class to have moved. So the paper argues we need a label-aware definition of a semantics-preserving perturbation - one that tracks the ground truth directly, rather than trusting a budget to protect it.
A reference classifier that knows the ground truth

The trouble with tracking ground truth is that on real data we don't have it after a perturbation - nobody labeled the graph you just edited. The paper's key move is to run the controlled experiments on Contextual Stochastic Block Models (CSBMs), a synthetic graph family where the data-generating process is known exactly. On a CSBM you can derive the Bayes optimal classifier g, which by construction outputs the most likely true class given the (possibly perturbed) graph. That g becomes a trusted reference for what the semantics actually are.

With a reference in hand, over-robustness has a crisp definition. Take a model f and a node v. On the clean graph, f and the reference g agree. Now apply a perturbation within the allowed budget. If that perturbation flips g - the true class has genuinely changed - but f keeps its original prediction, then f is over-robust at v: it is holding on to an answer that is now wrong. Figure 2 draws the picture. The model f defends a decision region (the hatched area) that extends past the true boundary drawn by g, and the perturbation balls B around each node reach across that true boundary.

en.caption: Figure 2. (a) The reference classifier g draws the true decision boundary (solid line); the model f defends a wider region (dotted), and the hatched strip in between is exactly where f stays robust after the semantics have changed. (b) Each node carries a finite perturbation set B; where those balls cross g's boundary, a "small" edit has already changed the node's true class.

en.text: To turn this into a number, the authors compare two notions of robustness for the same model. R(f) is conventional, degree-corrected robustness: how much perturbation f withstands before changing its prediction, measured against the node's original label. R(f, g) is semantics-aware robustness: the same quantity measured against the reference g, so it only counts robustness up to the point where the semantics actually change. Over-robustness is what conventional robustness claims that the semantics-aware version does not support: R_over = 1 - R(f, g) / R(f). A value of 0.2 means that one fifth of what we counted as the model's robustness actually lies beyond the point of semantic change, and should not have counted as robustness at all.
The experimental setup

The controlled experiments use CSBMs with n = 1000 nodes, parametrized to mimic CORA - matching its expected within-class and between-class edge counts (p = 0.63%, q = 0.15%, average degree d = 21). A single knob, the signal strength K, controls how discriminative the node features are: at K = 0.1 the features are almost noise and the graph structure carries the signal, while at K = 5 the features alone suffice and structure becomes unnecessary. For each K the authors sample 10 training graphs, inductively add 1000 fresh test nodes per graph, and average. The synthetic findings are then checked on the real-world Cora-ML graph and on a Contextual Barabasi-Albert model with community structure (CBA).
How much of "robustness" is over-robustness?

The first result is about the threat models themselves, before any model is even blamed. Under a common per-node budget (degree-plus-two edits) at K = 1.0, 99.4% of target nodes admit at least one perturbed graph whose true label has changed. In other words, the standard perturbation sets are saturated with graphs that are not semantics-preserving at all - the very inputs on which we grade a model's robustness.

The second result is about the models. Every architecture tested - GCN, SGC, APPNP, GAT, GATv2, GraphSAGE - is significantly over-robust. To get a ceiling, the authors also measure an MLP, which ignores graph structure entirely and is therefore maximally robust to edge edits; it shows 43% over-robustness at K = 0.1 under the weak l2 attack. Every GNN clusters near that upper bound. Figure 3 shows the full sweep: over-robustness R_over is high at low K, where structure carries the signal and edits do the most semantic damage, and falls toward zero as K grows and the features alone decide the label.

en.caption: Figure 3. Over-robustness R_over versus signal strength K (x-axis runs 0.1 to 5.0). Solid curves are plain models; dashed curves add label propagation (+LP). (a) uses a per-node degree budget; (b) applies the attack with no budget restriction. Adding label propagation (dashed) pulls every curve down, and plain LP (tan) sits lowest of all.

en.text: A fix that costs nothing: label propagation

If over-robustness comes from a model clinging to a prediction after the neighborhood has changed, one remedy is to feed the model information it usually ignores at inference time: the labels it already saw during training. The authors combine each GNN's soft predictions with label propagation (label spreading), which diffuses the known training labels across the graph. The dashed curves in Figure 3 are the result - every model's over-robustness drops sharply, and label propagation on its own achieves the lowest over-robustness of any method in the study.

The important detail is that this comes for free. Adding label propagation does not reduce test accuracy, and it often improves genuine adversarial robustness while the graph structure still carries useful signal. Concretely, a GCN combined with label propagation at K = 0.5 falls to R_over = 20.9%. The effect survives stronger, targeted attacks too, though it never fully vanishes: under Nettack, a GCN at K = 0.5 still shows 11.4% over-robustness, and even a structure-blind MLP at K = 2 retains 19.2%. The table below collects the headline numbers.

rows: Nodes with a semantics-changing perturbation (K = 1.0, degree-plus-two budget)
Over-robustness of a maximally robust classifier (K = 0.1, l2-weak)
GCN + label propagation over-robustness (K = 0.5)
GCN over-robustness under Nettack (K = 0.5)
MLP over-robustness under Nettack (K = 2)

en.text: Does the synthetic story hold on a real graph?

The CSBM lets the authors compute a ground-truth reference, but the worry is always that synthetic conclusions stay synthetic. Figure 4 addresses this on the real-world Cora-ML graph: it plots how many structure perturbations it takes to change a trained GCN's prediction, grouped by a node's degree. Low-degree nodes flip after only a handful of edits, exactly the regime where a small budget can rewire the whole neighborhood - and precisely the nodes that dominate real graphs. The mechanism the paper isolates on CSBMs is visible on data nobody generated to order.

en.caption: Figure 4. On the real-world Cora-ML graph, the number of structure perturbations needed to flip a GCN's prediction, by node degree. Low-degree nodes - the large majority in real graphs - change after very few edits, the regime where a "small" budget can already alter a node's true class.

en.text: Why this reframes robustness for graphs

The takeaway is not that GNNs are secretly fine. It is that our yardstick has been double-counting. A large part of the robustness we measure is over-robustness - a model refusing to update after the node's true meaning has already changed - and conventional evaluations credit that stubbornness as good behavior. Once you measure against the semantics rather than the original label, the picture sharpens: the same edits that look like an attack on a well-defended model are, for many low-degree nodes, legitimate changes of class the model failed to follow.

Two consequences stand out. First, folding the training graph's label structure back into inference through label propagation is a cheap, effective way to cut over-robustness without giving up accuracy or true adversarial robustness. Second, the authors show that under a semantics-aware definition, inductively classifying a newly added node carries no robustness-accuracy tradeoff at all - the tension we thought was fundamental was partly an artifact of measuring robustness against a label that had already moved. The honest boundary is that all of this rests on having a trustworthy reference for the true class, which CSBMs provide by construction and real graphs do not; extending semantics-aware evaluation to fully real settings is the open problem the paper leaves on the table.

For anyone building or evaluating graph models, the practical message is concrete. Treat a small edit budget as a claim about semantics that needs checking, not a guarantee - especially for the low-degree nodes that make up most of a real graph. Report robustness against a semantics-aware reference wherever one is available, and consider label propagation as a nearly free addition that trims over-robustness without costing accuracy. More broadly, the paper is a reminder that a metric is only as trustworthy as the assumption underneath it - and on graphs, the assumption that a budgeted edit preserves a node's meaning had gone largely unexamined until this work put it to the test.

zh.text: 关于图神经网络（Graph Neural Network，GNN）有一个流行的说法：它们脆弱得可怕。只需改动几条边，一个看起来很准的模型就会突然改口。过去十年，对抗稳健性（adversarial robustness）研究几乎都把这种脆弱当成全部问题：攻击者做一个微小的、不改变含义的改动，能够守住原有预测的模型才是稳健、可信的那个。这篇来自慕尼黑工业大学、发表在 ICLR 2023 的论文指出，这套叙事悄悄假设了一件我们在图上从未真正验证过的事情：那个「小改动」是否真的保留了节点的含义。

这个假设其实很关键。一个对抗样本之所以「对抗」，前提是它没有改变输入的真实标签；否则，模型改变预测只是对一个真正不同的输入做出的正确反应。对图像来说，人可以扫一眼扰动后的图片，确认它还是一只猫。但图没有这种视觉检查手段，于是社区退而求其次，用一个代理指标：数一数插入或删除了多少条边，只要这个数目不超过 l0 预算，就把这次扰动叫作「小」。论文的核心观察是：在真实图上，大多数节点的邻居本就很少，即使是很小的边预算，也足以把一个节点彻底重连；而一旦重连了一个低度数节点，它的真实类别可能早就变了。
这样看，一个死守旧预测的模型，其实谈不上任何好的意义上的稳健。它只是对一个真值已经移动的输入固执地判错。作者给这种失效模式起了个名字：过度稳健（over-robustness），并给出了度量它的工具。他们的核心结论令人不安：所测试的每一个 GNN 都存在显著的过度稳健，而我们平时津津乐道的稳健性，有相当大一部分落在节点语义早已翻转的那一侧。

zh.caption: 图1 在合成的 CSBM 图上，虚线「语义边界」表示：对于给定度数的节点，平均需要多少次边改动才会真正翻转它的真实类别（即最可能的类别）。而每个 GNN（彩色曲线）都要等到远高于这条线时才改变自己的预测——两者之间那整片阴影区，就是模型在语义已经改变之后仍然保持的稳健性。

zh.text: 论文：https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.00851
项目主页：https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/daml/revisiting-robustness/
为什么「数改了几条边」还不够
图之所以棘手，是因为你没法像看扰动后的图像那样去检查一个扰动后的节点。已有工作试图把「数边」变得更讲究一些，加入一些代理约束——尽量保持度数分布不变、保持同质性（homophily）等等——好让扰动看起来「不易察觉」。但这些启发式都回避了真正定义对抗样本的那个问题：这次改动之后，节点的真实标签还在吗？
这个缺口之所以重要，源于真实图的一个朴素事实：它们由大量低度数节点主导。如果一个节点只有三个邻居，而你的预算允许改动三条边，你就能把它从原来的整个邻域里剥离，再接进一个全新的邻域。此时度数分布看上去毫无异常，节点的真实类别却可能已经改变。因此论文主张，我们需要一个「标签感知」的、对语义保持的扰动的定义——直接追踪真值，而不是指望一个预算去保护它。
一个知道真值的参考分类器

追踪真值的难点在于：在真实数据上，扰动之后我们并没有真值——没人给你刚刚改动过的图重新标注。论文的关键一步，是把可控实验放在上下文随机块模型（Contextual Stochastic Block Model，CSBM）上——这是一类数据生成过程完全已知的合成图。在 CSBM 上，可以推导出贝叶斯最优分类器 g，它按定义输出给定（可能被扰动的）图下最可能的真实类别。于是 g 就成了「语义到底是什么」的可信参考。

有了参考，过度稳健就有了清晰的定义。取一个模型 f 和一个节点 v：在干净图上，f 与参考 g 的判断一致；现在在允许的预算内施加一次扰动，如果这次扰动翻转了 g（真实类别确实变了），而 f 仍然保持它原来的预测，那么 f 在 v 处就是过度稳健的——它守着一个如今已经错了的答案。图2 把这件事画了出来：模型 f 所防守的决策区域（阴影部分）越过了 g 划定的真实边界，而每个节点周围的扰动集合 B 正好跨过了那条真实边界。
这里值得停一下，体会「过度稳健」为什么是个坏消息。常规评估会为一个从不改变预测的模型鼓掌，把它当成最稳健、最可信的那个；但如果它所面对的输入其实早已属于另一个类别，这种「岿然不动」就变成了系统性的判错——而且是被指标伪装成优点的判错。参考分类器 g 的价值，恰恰在于把两种情况区分开：真正应当保持不变的稳健，和早已越过真实边界、本不该再保持的「稳健」。

zh.caption: 图2 (a) 参考分类器 g 画出真实决策边界（实线），模型 f 防守一个更宽的区域（虚线），两者之间的阴影带正是 f 在语义已改变之后仍保持稳健的地方。(b) 每个节点带着一个有限扰动集合 B；这些「球」跨过 g 边界的地方，就意味着一次「小」改动其实已经改变了节点的真实类别。

zh.text: 要把它变成一个数值，作者为同一个模型比较了两种稳健性。R(f) 是常规的、经过度数校正的稳健性：相对于节点原始标签，f 在改变预测之前能承受多少扰动。R(f, g) 是语义感知稳健性：同样的量，但相对于参考 g 来测，因此只统计到语义真正改变为止的那部分稳健性。过度稳健就是常规稳健性中「语义感知版本不予支持」的那部分：R_over = 1 − R(f, g) / R(f)。取值 0.2 意味着模型所测稳健性中有五分之一属于语义已变之后的稳健。
实验设置

可控实验使用 n = 1000 个节点的 CSBM，其参数被调成模仿 CORA——匹配它的类内与类间期望边数（p = 0.63%，q = 0.15%，平均度数 d = 21）。一个旋钮，即信号强度 K，控制节点特征有多大区分度：K = 0.1 时特征几乎是噪声、信号主要由图结构承载；K = 5 时仅凭特征就足够、结构变得多余。对每个 K，作者采样 10 张训练图，并在每张图上以归纳（inductive）方式新增 1000 个测试节点后取平均。合成实验的结论随后在真实图 Cora-ML，以及带社区结构的上下文 Barabási–Albert 模型（CBA）上得到印证。
「稳健性」里有多少其实是过度稳健？
第一个结果，是关于威胁模型（threat model）本身的，甚至还没轮到怪罪任何模型。在一个常见的按节点预算（度数加二次改动）下，当 K = 1.0 时，99.4% 的目标节点都存在至少一张真实标签已经改变的扰动图。换句话说，标准扰动集合里充斥着根本不保持语义的图——而我们恰恰是在这些输入上给模型的稳健性打分。

第二个结果，是关于模型的。所测试的每一种架构——GCN、SGC、APPNP、GAT、GATv2、GraphSAGE——都存在显著的过度稳健。为了给出一个上界，作者还测了一个 MLP：它完全忽略图结构，因而对边改动天然最稳健；在 K = 0.1、弱 l2 攻击下，它表现出 43% 的过度稳健。而每个 GNN 都紧贴着这个上界聚集。图3 展示了完整的扫描：过度稳健 R_over 在低 K 时很高——此时信号靠结构承载，边改动造成的语义破坏最大——并随着 K 增大、特征本身足以决定标签而趋近于零。

zh.caption: 图3 过度稳健 R_over 随信号强度 K 变化（横轴从 0.1 到 5.0）。实线为原始模型，虚线为叠加标签传播（+LP）后的模型。(a) 采用按节点度数的预算；(b) 不设预算限制地施加攻击。加入标签传播（虚线）把每条曲线都往下拉，而单独的 LP（浅棕色）位于所有方法的最低处。

zh.text: 一个几乎零成本的修法：标签传播
如果过度稳健来自模型在邻域已变之后仍死守预测，那么一个补救办法，就是在推理时喂给模型它平时忽略的信息：它在训练时早已见过的标签。作者把每个 GNN 的软预测与标签传播（label propagation / label spreading）结合起来，让已知的训练标签沿图扩散开去。图3 中的虚线就是结果——每个模型的过度稳健都大幅下降，而单独使用标签传播，取得了本研究中所有方法里最低的过度稳健。

关键细节是：这几乎是免费的。加入标签传播不会降低测试准确率，而且在图结构仍然携带有用信号时，往往还会提升真正的对抗稳健性。具体来说，GCN 叠加标签传播后，在 K = 0.5 时过度稳健降到 R_over = 20.9%。这一效果在更强的定向攻击下依然存在，只是无法完全消除：在 Nettack 下，K = 0.5 的 GCN 仍有 11.4% 的过度稳健，即便是对结构视而不见的 MLP，在 K = 2 时也还残留 19.2%。下面的表格汇总了这些关键数字。

rows: 存在改变语义的扰动的节点比例（K = 1.0，度数加二 预算）

zh.text: 合成结论在真实图上成立吗？
CSBM 让作者能算出真值参考，但一个始终存在的担忧是：合成的结论会不会只停留在合成世界里。图4 在真实图 Cora-ML 上回应了这一点：它画出把一个训练好的 GCN 的预测翻转所需的结构扰动次数，并按节点度数分组。低度数节点只需寥寥几次改动就会翻转——正是「小预算即可重连整个邻域」的那种情形，也正是主导真实图的那类节点。论文在 CSBM 上分离出的机制，在没人刻意生成的数据上同样清晰可见。

zh.caption: 图4 在真实图 Cora-ML 上，按节点度数统计翻转 GCN 预测所需的结构扰动次数。低度数节点——在真实图中占绝大多数——只需很少的改动就会翻转，正是「小」预算已足以改变节点真实类别的区间。

zh.text: 为什么这重新定义了图上的稳健性
结论并不是说 GNN 其实没问题，而是说我们的尺子一直在重复计数。我们所测稳健性里有很大一部分是过度稳健——模型在节点真实含义已经改变之后拒绝更新——而常规评估把这种固执当成了好行为。一旦改为相对语义而非原始标签来度量，图景就清晰了：那些看似在攻击一个防守严密模型的改动，对许多低度数节点来说，其实是模型没能跟上的、合理的类别变化。
有两点尤其值得记住。其一，通过标签传播把训练图的标签结构折回推理，是一个廉价而有效的办法，能在不牺牲准确率和真实对抗稳健性的前提下削减过度稳健。其二，作者证明：在语义感知的定义下，以归纳方式给一个新加入的节点分类，根本不存在稳健性与准确率的权衡——我们以为根本性的那种张力，部分只是「相对一个早已移动的标签去度量稳健性」造成的假象。
当然，这一切都依赖于一个可信的真值参考：CSBM 按构造提供了它，真实图却没有，如何把语义感知的评估推广到完全真实的场景，是论文留在桌上的开放问题。对实践者而言，启示也很直接：把小的边预算当成一个需要验证的语义假设，而不是理所当然的保证，并把标签传播当成一个几乎免费、却能削减过度稳健的补充。

en.subtitle: A semantics-aware look at adversarial robustness from TU Munich, and why a large part of what we call GNN robustness is robustness we should not want

zh.title: ICLR 2023 | 图神经网络不只是脆弱，它们还「过度稳健」
zh.subtitle: 慕尼黑工业大学重新审视图机器学习的对抗稳健性：当我们说的「小扰动」其实早已改变了节点的真实标签

en.text: The standard story about graph neural networks (GNNs) is that they are dangerously easy to fool. Flip a handful of edges, and a model that looked accurate suddenly changes its mind. A decade of adversarial-robustness research has treated that fragility as the whole problem: the attacker makes a tiny, meaning-preserving change, and the model that keeps its prediction is the robust, trustworthy one. This ICLR 2023 paper from the Technical University of Munich points out that the story quietly assumes something we never actually check on graphs - that the small change really did preserve the node's meaning.

That assumption is doing a lot of work. An adversarial example is only adversarial if it leaves the input's true label untouched; otherwise a changed prediction is just a correct response to a genuinely different input. For images, a human can glance at the perturbed picture and confirm it still shows a cat. Graphs have no such visual check, so the community settled on a proxy: count how many edges were inserted or deleted, and call the perturbation "small" if that count stays under an l0 budget. The paper's central observation is that on real graphs, where most nodes have very few neighbors, even a tiny edge budget can rewire a node completely - and once you rewire a low-degree node, its true class may have already changed.

Read that way, a model that stubbornly keeps its old prediction is not being robust in any good sense. It is being wrong about an input whose ground truth has moved. The authors give this failure mode a name - over-robustness - and build the tools to measure it. Their headline finding is uncomfortable: every GNN they test is significantly over-robust, and a surprisingly large share of the robustness we routinely celebrate lies beyond the point where the node's semantics already flipped.

Every GNN (colored curves) only changes its own prediction far above that line - the entire shaded band between the two is robustness the model keeps after the semantics have already changed.

zh.text: 关于图神经网络（Graph Neural Network，GNN）有一个流行的说法：它们脆弱得可怕。只需改动几条边，一个看起来很准的模型就会突然改口。过去十年，对抗稳健性（adversarial robustness）研究几乎都把这种脆弱当成全部问题：攻击者做一个微小的、不改变含义的改动，能够守住原有预测的模型才是稳健、可信的那个。这篇来自慕尼黑工业大学、发表在 ICLR 2023 的论文指出，这套叙事悄悄假设了一件我们在图上从未真正验证过的事情：那个「小改动」是否真的保留了节点的含义。

这个假设其实很关键。一个对抗样本之所以「对抗」，前提是它没有改变输入的真实标签；否则，模型改变预测只是对一个真正不同的输入做出的正确反应。对图像来说，人可以扫一眼扰动后的图片，确认它还是一只猫。但图没有这种视觉检查手段，于是社区退而求其次，用一个代理指标：数一数插入或删除了多少条边，只要这个数目不超过 l0 预算，就把这次扰动叫作「小」。论文的核心观察是：在真实图上，大多数节点的邻居本就很少，即使是很小的边预算，也足以把一个节点彻底重连；而一旦重连了一个低度数节点，它的真实类别可能早就变了。
这样看，一个死守旧预测的模型，其实谈不上任何好的意义上的稳健。它只是对一个真值已经移动的输入固执地判错。作者给这种失效模式起了个名字：过度稳健（over-robustness），并给出了度量它的工具。他们的核心结论令人不安：所测试的每一个 GNN 都存在显著的过度稳健，而我们平时津津乐道的稳健性，有相当大一部分落在节点语义早已翻转的那一侧。

zh.caption: 图1 在合成的 CSBM 图上，虚线「语义边界」表示：对于给定度数的节点，平均需要多少次边改动才会真正翻转它的真实类别（即最可能的类别）。而每个 GNN（彩色曲线）都要等到远高于这条线时才改变自己的预测——两者之间那整片阴影区，就是模型在语义已经改变之后仍然保持的稳健性。

en.caption: Figure 1. On synthetic CSBM graphs, the dotted "semantic boundary" marks how many edge changes actually flip a node's true (most-likely) class, as a function of node degree. Every GNN (colored curves) only changes its own prediction far above that line - the entire shaded band between the two is robustness the model keeps after the semantics have already changed.

en.text: Why "count the edited edges" is not enough

The reason graphs are hard is that you cannot inspect a perturbed node the way you inspect a perturbed image. Prior work tried to make edge-counting more principled by adding proxies - keep the degree distribution roughly fixed, preserve homophily, and so on - so that a perturbation looks "unnoticeable." But none of those heuristics asks the one question that actually defines an adversarial example: did the node's ground-truth label survive the edit?

This gap matters because of a plain fact about real graphs: they are dominated by low-degree nodes. If a node has three neighbors and your budget lets you change three edges, you can detach it from its entire original neighborhood and wire it into a new one. Nothing about the degree distribution needs to look suspicious for the node's true class to have moved. So the paper argues we need a label-aware definition of a semantics-preserving perturbation - one that tracks the ground truth directly, rather than trusting a budget to protect it.

zh.text: 为什么「数改了几条边」还不够
图之所以棘手，是因为你没法像看扰动后的图像那样去检查一个扰动后的节点。已有工作试图把「数边」变得更讲究一些，加入一些代理约束——尽量保持度数分布不变、保持同质性（homophily）等等——好让扰动看起来「不易察觉」。但这些启发式都回避了真正定义对抗样本的那个问题：这次改动之后，节点的真实标签还在吗？
这个缺口之所以重要，源于真实图的一个朴素事实：它们由大量低度数节点主导。如果一个节点只有三个邻居，而你的预算允许改动三条边，你就能把它从原来的整个邻域里剥离，再接进一个全新的邻域。此时度数分布看上去毫无异常，节点的真实类别却可能已经改变。因此论文主张，我们需要一个「标签感知」的、对语义保持的扰动的定义——直接追踪真值，而不是指望一个预算去保护它。

zh.title: ICLR 2023 | 图神经网络不只是脆弱，它们还「过度稳健」
zh.subtitle: 慕尼黑工业大学重新审视图机器学习的对抗稳健性：当我们说的「小扰动」其实早已改变了节点的真实标签

en.text: A reference classifier that knows the ground truth

The trouble with tracking ground truth is that on real data we don't have it after a perturbation - nobody labeled the graph you just edited. The paper's key move is to run the controlled experiments on Contextual Stochastic Block Models (CSBMs), a synthetic graph family where the data-generating process is known exactly. On a CSBM you can derive the Bayes optimal classifier g, which by construction outputs the most likely true class given the (possibly perturbed) graph. That g becomes a trusted reference for what the semantics actually are.

With a reference in hand, over-robustness has a crisp definition. Take a model f and a node v. On the clean graph, f and the reference g agree. Now apply a perturbation within the allowed budget. If that perturbation flips g - the true class has genuinely changed - but f keeps its original prediction, then f is over-robust at v: it is holding on to an answer that is now wrong. Figure 2 draws the picture. The model f defends a decision region (the hatched area) that extends past the true boundary drawn by g, and the perturbation balls B around each node reach across that true boundary.

en.caption: Figure 2. (a) The reference classifier g draws the true decision boundary (solid line); the model f defends a wider region (dotted), and the hatched strip in between is exactly where f stays robust after the semantics have changed. (b) Each node carries a finite perturbation set B; where those balls cross g's boundary, a "small" edit has already changed the node's true class.

en.text: To turn this into a number, the authors compare two notions of robustness for the same model. R(f) is conventional, degree-corrected robustness: how much perturbation f withstands before changing its prediction, measured against the node's original label. R(f, g) is semantics-aware robustness: the same quantity measured against the reference g, so it only counts robustness up to the point where the semantics actually change. Over-robustness is what conventional robustness claims that the semantics-aware version does not support: R_over = 1 - R(f, g) / R(f). A value of 0.2 means that one fifth of what we counted as the model's robustness actually lies beyond the point of semantic change, and should not have counted as robustness at all.

zh.text: 一个知道真值的参考分类器

追踪真值的难点在于：在真实数据上，扰动之后我们并没有真值——没人给你刚刚改动过的图重新标注。论文的关键一步，是把可控实验放在上下文随机块模型（Contextual Stochastic Block Model，CSBM）上——这是一类数据生成过程完全已知的合成图。在 CSBM 上，可以推导出贝叶斯最优分类器 g，它按定义输出给定（可能被扰动的）图下最可能的真实类别。于是 g 就成了「语义到底是什么」的可信参考。

有了参考，过度稳健就有了清晰的定义。取一个模型 f 和一个节点 v：在干净图上，f 与参考 g 的判断一致；现在在允许的预算内施加一次扰动，如果这次扰动翻转了 g（真实类别确实变了），而 f 仍然保持它原来的预测，那么 f 在 v 处就是过度稳健的——它守着一个如今已经错了的答案。图2 把这件事画了出来：模型 f 所防守的决策区域（阴影部分）越过了 g 划定的真实边界，而每个节点周围的扰动集合 B 正好跨过了那条真实边界。
这里值得停一下，体会「过度稳健」为什么是个坏消息。常规评估会为一个从不改变预测的模型鼓掌，把它当成最稳健、最可信的那个；但如果它所面对的输入其实早已属于另一个类别，这种「岿然不动」就变成了系统性的判错——而且是被指标伪装成优点的判错。参考分类器 g 的价值，恰恰在于把两种情况区分开：真正应当保持不变的稳健，和早已越过真实边界、本不该再保持的「稳健」。

zh.caption: 图2 (a) 参考分类器 g 画出真实决策边界（实线），模型 f 防守一个更宽的区域（虚线），两者之间的阴影带正是 f 在语义已改变之后仍保持稳健的地方。(b) 每个节点带着一个有限扰动集合 B；这些「球」跨过 g 边界的地方，就意味着一次「小」改动其实已经改变了节点的真实类别。

zh.text: 要把它变成一个数值，作者为同一个模型比较了两种稳健性。R(f) 是常规的、经过度数校正的稳健性：相对于节点原始标签，f 在改变预测之前能承受多少扰动。R(f, g) 是语义感知稳健性：同样的量，但相对于参考 g 来测，因此只统计到语义真正改变为止的那部分稳健性。过度稳健就是常规稳健性中「语义感知版本不予支持」的那部分：R_over = 1 − R(f, g) / R(f)。取值 0.2 意味着模型所测稳健性中有五分之一属于语义已变之后的稳健。

第一个结果，是关于威胁模型（threat model）本身的，甚至还没轮到怪罪任何模型。在一个常见的按节点预算（度数加二次改动）下，当 K = 1.0 时，99.4% 的目标节点都存在至少一张真实标签已经改变的扰动图。换句话说，标准扰动集合里充斥着根本不保持语义的图——而我们恰恰是在这些输入上给模型的稳健性打分。

zh.caption: 图3 过度稳健 R_over 随信号强度 K 变化（横轴从 0.1 到 5.0）。实线为原始模型，虚线为叠加标签传播（+LP）后的模型。(a) 采用按节点度数的预算；(b) 不设预算限制地施加攻击。加入标签传播（虚线）把每条曲线都往下拉，而单独的 LP（浅棕色）位于所有方法的最低处。

zh.text: 一个几乎零成本的修法：标签传播
如果过度稳健来自模型在邻域已变之后仍死守预测，那么一个补救办法，就是在推理时喂给模型它平时忽略的信息：它在训练时早已见过的标签。作者把每个 GNN 的软预测与标签传播（label propagation / label spreading）结合起来，让已知的训练标签沿图扩散开去。图3 中的虚线就是结果——每个模型的过度稳健都大幅下降，而单独使用标签传播，取得了本研究中所有方法里最低的过度稳健。

关键细节是：这几乎是免费的。加入标签传播不会降低测试准确率，而且在图结构仍然携带有用信号时，往往还会提升真正的对抗稳健性。具体来说，GCN 叠加标签传播后，在 K = 0.5 时过度稳健降到 R_over = 20.9%。这一效果在更强的定向攻击下依然存在，只是无法完全消除：在 Nettack 下，K = 0.5 的 GCN 仍有 11.4% 的过度稳健，即便是对结构视而不见的 MLP，在 K = 2 时也还残留 19.2%。下面的表格汇总了这些关键数字。

en.text: How much of "robustness" is over-robustness?

The first result is about the threat models themselves, before any model is even blamed. Under a common per-node budget (degree-plus-two edits) at K = 1.0, 99.4% of target nodes admit at least one perturbed graph whose true label has changed. In other words, the standard perturbation sets are saturated with graphs that are not semantics-preserving at all - the very inputs on which we grade a model's robustness.

The second result is about the models. Every architecture tested - GCN, SGC, APPNP, GAT, GATv2, GraphSAGE - is significantly over-robust. To get a ceiling, the authors also measure an MLP, which ignores graph structure entirely and is therefore maximally robust to edge edits; it shows 43% over-robustness at K = 0.1 under the weak l2 attack. Every GNN clusters near that upper bound. Figure 3 shows the full sweep: over-robustness R_over is high at low K, where structure carries the signal and edits do the most semantic damage, and falls toward zero as K grows and the features alone decide the label.

en.caption: Figure 3. Over-robustness R_over versus signal strength K (x-axis runs 0.1 to 5.0). Solid curves are plain models; dashed curves add label propagation (+LP). (a) uses a per-node degree budget; (b) applies the attack with no budget restriction. Adding label propagation (dashed) pulls every curve down, and plain LP (tan) sits lowest of all.

en.text: A fix that costs nothing: label propagation

If over-robustness comes from a model clinging to a prediction after the neighborhood has changed, one remedy is to feed the model information it usually ignores at inference time: the labels it already saw during training. The authors combine each GNN's soft predictions with label propagation (label spreading), which diffuses the known training labels across the graph. The dashed curves in Figure 3 are the result - every model's over-robustness drops sharply, and label propagation on its own achieves the lowest over-robustness of any method in the study.

The important detail is that this comes for free. Adding label propagation does not reduce test accuracy, and it often improves genuine adversarial robustness while the graph structure still carries useful signal. Concretely, a GCN combined with label propagation at K = 0.5 falls to R_over = 20.9%. The effect survives stronger, targeted attacks too, though it never fully vanishes: under Nettack, a GCN at K = 0.5 still shows 11.4% over-robustness, and even a structure-blind MLP at K = 2 retains 19.2%. Second, the authors show that under a semantics-aware definition, inductively classifying a newly added node carries no robustness-accuracy tradeoff at all - the tension we thought was fundamental was partly an artifact of measuring robustness against a label that had already moved. en.text: Why "count the edited edges" is not enough

The reason graphs are hard is that you cannot inspect a perturbed node the way you inspect a perturbed image. This gap matters because of a plain fact about real graphs: they are dominated by low-degree nodes. If a node has three neighbors and your budget lets you change three edges, you can detach it from its entire original neighborhood and wire it into a new one. Nothing about the degree distribution needs to look suspicious for the node's true class to have moved. So the paper argues we need a label-aware definition of a semantics-preserving perturbation - one that tracks the ground truth directly, rather than trusting a budget to protect it.

This ICLR 2023 paper from the Technical University of Munich points out that the story quietly assumes something we never actually check on graphs - that the small change really did preserve the node's meaning.

That assumption is doing a lot of work. An adversarial example is only adversarial if it leaves the input's true label untouched; otherwise a changed prediction is just a correct response to a genuinely different input. For images, a human can glance at the perturbed picture and confirm it still shows a cat. Graphs have no such visual check, so the community settled on a proxy: count how many edges were inserted or deleted, and call the perturbation "small" if that count stays under an l0 budget. The paper's central observation is that on real graphs, where most nodes have very few neighbors, even a tiny edge budget can rewire a node completely - and once you rewire a low-degree node, its true class may have already changed.

Read that way, a model that stubbornly keeps its old prediction is not being robust in any good sense. It is being wrong about an input whose ground truth has moved. The authors give this failure mode a name - over-robustness - and build the tools to measure it. Their headline finding is uncomfortable: every GNN they test is significantly over-robust, and a surprisingly large share of the robustness we routinely celebrate lies beyond the point where the node's semantics already flipped.

zh.text: 关于图神经网络（Graph Neural Network，GNN）有一个流行的说法：它们脆弱得可怕。只需改动几条边，一个看起来很准的模型就会突然改口。过去十年，对抗稳健性（adversarial robustness）研究几乎都把这种脆弱当成全部问题：攻击者做一个微小的、不改变含义的改动，能够守住原有预测的模型才是稳健、可信的那个。这篇来自慕尼黑工业大学、发表在 ICLR 2023 的论文指出，这套叙事悄悄假设了一件我们在图上从未真正验证过的事情：那个「小改动」是否真的保留了节点的含义。

这个假设其实很关键。一个对抗样本之所以「对抗」，前提是它没有改变输入的真实标签；否则，模型改变预测只是对一个真正不同的输入做出的正确反应。对图像来说，人可以扫一眼扰动后的图片，确认它还是一只猫。但图没有这种视觉检查手段，于是社区退而求其次，用一个代理指标：数一数插入或删除了多少条边，只要这个数目不超过 l0 预算，就把这次扰动叫作「小」。论文的核心观察是：在真实图上，大多数节点的邻居本就很少，即使是很小的边预算，也足以把一个节点彻底重连；而一旦重连了一个低度数节点，它的真实类别可能早就变了。
这样看，一个死守旧预测的模型，其实谈不上任何好的意义上的稳健。它只是对一个真值已经移动的输入固执地判错。作者给这种失效模式起了个名字：过度稳健（over-robustness），并给出了度量它的工具。他们的核心结论令人不安：所测试的每一个 GNN 都存在显著的过度稳健，而我们平时津津乐道的稳健性，有相当大一部分落在节点语义早已翻转的那一侧。

项目主页：https://www.cs.cit.tum.de/daml/revisiting-robustness/
实验设置

可控实验使用 n = 1000 个节点的 CSBM，其参数被调成模仿 CORA——匹配它的类内与类间期望边数（p = 0.63%，q = 0.15%，平均度数 d = 21）。一个旋钮，即信号强度 K，控制节点特征有多大区分度：K = 0.1 时特征几乎是噪声、信号主要由图结构承载；K = 5 时仅凭特征就足够、结构变得多余。对每个 K，作者采样 10 张训练图，并在每张图上以归纳（inductive）方式新增 1000 个测试节点后取平均。合成实验的结论随后在真实图 Cora-ML，以及带社区结构的上下文 Barabási–Albert 模型（CBA）上得到印证。
